vo_text: Venus is the planet most like Earth. So what happened to it?
This is the ground on Venus seen through the clouds by radar. Why radar?
Because ordinary light cannot get through. It is hot enough to melt lead.
The air presses down like the sea nearly a kilometer deep. No machine we have
landed there could survive it for much more than two hours.
And this world is almost the size of yours. It is made of the same rock. It
even takes in less sunlight than Earth does, and it is still the hottest planet in the solar system.
In this film, I will show you how that can be true, where its water went, and why the answer is still open.

Less light in and still a surface at four hundred and sixty-five degrees.
It sounds like a paradox. It stops being one when you look at the air.
So the heat is not about how much light arrives. It is about what happens to the heat
once it is there. It cannot get out.
What would you see if you stood there? Not darkness. The clouds let through a dim orange daylight like a heavy evening that never ends.
You would never see the sun itself. The wind at the ground moves at little more than a slow walk. But in air that thick, even a slow wind pushes like a river.
